subject: medicine
title: Rhabdomyolysis, myoglobinuric acute kidney injury, and dialysis indications

steps.tx: Massive skeletal muscle necrosis following traumatic crush injury, prolonged immobility, extreme exertion, or drug toxicity releases toxic intracellular constituents into the systemic circulation. Presenting as **rhabdomyolysis**, the clinical syndrome features muscle tenderness, weakness, and dark tea-coloured urine. Serum creatine kinase elevations exceeding five to ten times the upper reference limit (frequently rising beyond ten thousand units per litre) establish the diagnosis. Accompanying hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hyperuricaemia, and early hypocalcaemia from calcium precipitation into damaged myocytes create life-threatening systemic electrolyte disturbances.
steps.say: Massive skeletal muscle necrosis following crush trauma, immobility, or drug toxicity releases toxic intracellular contents into the bloodstream. Presenting as rhabdomyolysis, this condition features muscular pain, weakness, and dark tea-coloured urine. Marked serum creatine kinase elevation establishes the diagnosis, accompanied by dangerous hyperkalaemia and hyperphosphataemia.

steps.tx: Extensive release of filtered low-molecular-weight monomeric heme pigments provokes acute intrarenal vasoconstriction and direct tubular damage. Developing **myoglobinuria** produces orthotolidine dipstick positivity for blood in the complete absence of intact erythrocytes on microscopic examination. In the setting of systemic volume depletion and aciduria, ferrihemate precipitates with Tamm-Horsfall mucoprotein within distal nephron segments, forming obstructing tubular casts. Direct oxidative lipid peroxidation of proximal tubular cell membranes compounds the damage, mandating immediate aggressive volume expansion with isotonic crystalloids (three to five hundred millilitres per hour).
steps.say: Extensive filtration of muscle heme pigments causes renal vasoconstriction and direct tubular damage. Developing myoglobinuria produces positive urine dipstick results for blood without any intact red blood cells on microscopy. In acidic urine, myoglobin precipitates to form obstructing casts, requiring aggressive early hydration with isotonic intravenous fluids.

steps.tx: Direct accumulation of polycationic antimicrobial agents within proximal tubular lysosomes provokes iatrogenic intrinsic renal parenchymal injury. Manifesting as **aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity**, agents such as gentamicin, amikacin, and tobramycin bind anionic phospholipids on the brush border, undergoing endocytosis into lysosomal compartments where they disrupt membrane permeability. Characteristically presenting as non-oliguric acute tubular necrosis seven to ten days after drug initiation, progressive rise in serum creatinine coincides with wasting of magnesium and calcium. Therapeutic drug monitoring of peak and trough serum concentrations minimizes toxicity.
steps.say: Direct accumulation of antimicrobial agents within proximal tubular lysosomes causes iatrogenic kidney damage. Manifesting as aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity, drugs like gentamicin enter proximal tubular cells and disrupt membrane permeability. This presentation causes non-oliguric acute tubular necrosis after one week of treatment, requiring therapeutic drug level monitoring.

left.title: Aminoglycoside Nephrotoxicity
points: Non-oliguric acute tubular necrosis
Delayed onset 7 to 10 days into therapy
Toxicity correlates with elevated trough levels
Associated with hypomagnesaemia and hypokalaemia

right.title: Radiocontrast Nephropathy
points: Oliguric or non-oliguric tubular injury
Rapid onset within 24 to 48 hours of exposure
Creatinine peaks at 3 to 5 days, recovers in 7 to 10
Mitigated by pre-procedure isotonic hydration

steps.tx: Mechanical impedance to urinary drainage anywhere along the collecting system from the renal pelvis down to the urethral meatus provokes bilateral parenchymal pressure elevation. Clinically termed **obstructive uropathy**, common aetiologies include benign prostatic hyperplasia, bilateral ureteral lithiasis, retroperitoneal fibrosis, and pelvic malignancies. Prompt bedside ultrasound demonstrates pelvicalyceal dilatation (hydronephrosis) in over ninety percent of cases, although early acute obstruction or retroperitoneal encasement can yield false-negative non-dilated imaging. Bladder catheterization or percutaneous nephrostomy placement achieves rapid decompression, frequently followed by post-obstructive diuresis.
steps.say: Mechanical impedance to urinary drainage along the collecting system causes bilateral intrarenal pressure elevation. Clinically termed obstructive uropathy, common causes include prostatic enlargement, ureteric calculi, and pelvic tumours. Renal ultrasound demonstrates pelvicalyceal dilatation in most cases, while urgent catheterization or nephrostomy relieves the obstruction.

rows: Spinal cord injury, diabetic autonomic neuropathy

steps.tx: Monitoring dynamic 24-hour urinary output provides immediate bedside stratification of nephron filtration failure and clinical prognosis. Defining pathological **oliguria** requires a total 24-hour urine volume below four hundred millilitres in adults (or under zero point five millilitres per kilogram per hour for over six hours), representing the minimum volume needed to excrete daily obligatory solute loads. Complete absence of urine (anuria under one hundred millilitres daily) points toward total urinary tract obstruction, catastrophic cortical necrosis, or bilateral renal artery occlusion.
steps.say: Monitoring daily urine output provides rapid bedside stratification of filtration failure and clinical prognosis. Defining pathological oliguria requires a daily urine volume under four hundred millilitres, reflecting failure to clear obligatory solute loads. Complete anuria indicates total urinary tract obstruction, bilateral vascular occlusion, or cortical necrosis.

left.title: Oliguric Acute Kidney Injury
points: Urine volume < 400 mL/day (<0.5 mL/kg/h)
Severe tubular injury or advanced hypoperfusion
High incidence of hyperkalaemia and volume overload
Carries higher hospital mortality and dialysis requirement

right.title: Non-Oliguric Acute Kidney Injury
points: Urine volume > 400 mL/day despite rising creatinine
Common in aminoglycoside and interstitial injury
Preserved fluid clearance eases nutritional management
More favourable spontaneous recovery trajectory

steps.tx: Differential tubular reabsorption of urea relative to creatinine provides valuable diagnostic discrimination between renal hypoperfusion and structural parenchymal damage. Calculating the **BUN creatinine ratio** in prerenal azotaemia demonstrates an elevated ratio exceeding twenty to one, because enhanced proximal tubular sodium and water reabsorption stimulates passive back-diffusion of urea, while non-reabsorbed creatinine remains trapped in urine. Conversely, in acute tubular necrosis, necrotic epithelial damage disrupts passive back-diffusion, maintaining the ratio at normal baseline levels between ten to one and fifteen to one.
steps.say: Differential tubular handling of urea relative to creatinine helps distinguish renal hypoperfusion from parenchymal damage. Calculating the BUN creatinine ratio in prerenal failure shows values exceeding twenty to one, because sluggish tubular flow enhances passive urea reabsorption. In acute tubular necrosis, tubular damage prevents back-diffusion, keeping the ratio near ten to one.

rows: Increased proximal tubular passive urea reabsorption
Volume contraction, heart failure, renal artery stenosis
Ischemic or toxic tubular epithelial necrosis
Increased protein catabolism or urea generation
Upper GI bleed, high-dose glucocorticoids, catabolism
Diminished urea synthesis or severe muscle release
Severe liver disease, starvation, advanced rhabdomyolysis

steps.tx: Life-threatening metabolic derangements refractory to conservative medical management dictate urgent initiation of renal replacement therapy. Standard emergency **dialysis indications** follow the classic AEIOU framework: severe refractory metabolic Acidosis (pH under seven point one five), refractory hyperkalaemic Electrolyte toxicity (serum potassium exceeding six point five milliequivalents per litre with cardiac conduction abnormalities), dialyzable Ingestions (methanol, ethylene glycol, lithium, salicylates), refractory volume Overload manifesting as pulmonary oedema, and symptomatic Uraemia manifesting as pericarditis, encephalopathy, or platelet dysfunction.
steps.say: Severe metabolic derangements unresponsive to medical therapy require urgent renal replacement initiation. Standard emergency dialysis indications follow the classic AEIOU framework, encompassing refractory acidosis, hyperkalaemia with cardiac toxicity, toxic alcohol ingestions, refractory pulmonary oedema, and symptomatic uraemic complications like pericarditis or encephalopathy.

nodes.label: Refractory Acidosis, Hyperkalaemia, Toxic Ingestion, Volume Overload, Uraemia

steps.tx: Selecting the optimal renal replacement modality in acute kidney failure depends upon patient haemodynamic stability and vascular access. Implementing **renal replacement modality selection** directs haemodynamically stable ward patients toward intermittent haemodialysis, which achieves rapid solute clearance and fluid removal over three to four hours. Conversely, critically ill patients with septic or cardiogenic shock require continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), such as continuous venovenous haemodiafiltration. Slower continuous ultrafiltration avoids abrupt arterial pressure drops, preserving cerebral and coronary perfusion while preventing recurrent ischemic renal insults.
steps.say: Selecting the optimal renal replacement modality in acute kidney failure depends on patient haemodynamic stability. Implementing renal replacement modality selection directs stable patients toward intermittent haemodialysis for rapid solute removal. In unstable intensive care patients, continuous renal replacement therapy provides gentle ultrafiltration that preserves blood pressure and organ perfusion.

left.title: Intermittent Haemodialysis (IHD)
points: Rapid solute and fluid removal over 3 to 4 hours
Preferred in haemodynamically stable patients
Risk of rapid fluid shifts and hypotension
Lower cost and flexible scheduling

right.title: Continuous Renal Replacement (CRRT)
points: Continuous ultrafiltration over 24 hours
Preferred in shock and intracranial hypertension
Avoids abrupt arterial hypotension and cerebral oedema
Requires continuous anticoagulation (citrate/heparin)
